reminder: A real algebraic curve is the set of real solutions of a polynomial equation in two variables with real coefficients.
definition: A real [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) is a curve defined by [polynomial](c:polynomial) equations with coefficients in the [real numbers](c:real-number). In the plane it is the zero set of a nonzero real polynomial $f(x,y)$, and its real points are the points $(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $f(x,y)=0$.
examples: The circle $x^2+y^2=1$ is a real algebraic curve of degree 2.
The cubic $y^2=x^3-x$ has a real part with two pieces: a bounded oval and an unbounded branch.
Non-example: the graph of $y=\sin x$ is not a real algebraic curve, because no nonzero polynomial $f(x,y)$ vanishes on all of it.

steps: Take a nonzero polynomial $f$ with real coefficients.
Read the equation $f=0$ over the complex numbers to get an algebraic curve.
This curve is defined over the real numbers, and its real points form the real algebraic curve.
links.why: The degree and the genus of the complex curve control the shape of the real curve, as in Harnack's theorem.

reminder: The real projective space $\mathbb{R}P^n$ is the set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
definition: The real projective space $\mathbb{R}P^n$ is the [projective space](c:projective-space) of the [vector space](c:vector-space) $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$; its points are the one-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Equivalently, it is the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}$ by the relation $v\sim\lambda v$ for $\lambda\neq0$, or the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ with each point identified with its antipode.
examples: $\mathbb{R}P^1$ is the set of lines through the origin of the plane; it is a circle.
$\mathbb{R}P^2$ is the real projective plane, a closed surface that is not orientable.
Non-example: the sphere $S^n$ is not $\mathbb{R}P^n$; it is a double cover, because $x$ and $-x$ are two points of $S^n$ but one point of $\mathbb{R}P^n$.

steps: Take the field of scalars to be $\mathbb{R}$.
Take the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
Its projective space has the lines through the origin as points, so it is $\mathbb{R}P^n$.
links.why: General facts about projective spaces, such as homogeneous coordinates, apply to $\mathbb{R}P^n$.

steps: Set $n=2$ in the definition of $\mathbb{R}P^n$.
The points are then the lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
This space is the real projective plane.
links.why: The plane is the first case of the family of spaces $\mathbb{R}P^n$ that learners meet in topology.

reminder: A real root of a polynomial is a real number at which the polynomial equals zero.
definition: A real root of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ with real coefficients is a [real number](c:real-number) $r$ with $p(r)=0$. Its multiplicity is the largest $m$ such that $(x-r)^m$ divides $p$.
examples: $x^2-2$ has the two real roots $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$.
$(x-1)^3$ has one real root, $1$, with multiplicity 3.
Non-example: $x^2+1$ has no real root; its roots $i$ and $-i$ are not real numbers.

steps: Take a polynomial $p$ with real coefficients.
Call a number $r$ a root of $p$ when $p(r)=0$.
Add the condition that $r$ is a real number, not only a complex number.
links.why: Rules about real roots, such as Descartes' rule of signs, count only the roots on the real line.

reminder: A realizer of a formula in a model is an element that witnesses that the formula holds there.
definition: In a realizability semantics, each formula $\varphi$ has in a [model](c:model) a set of realizers, the elements that witness that $\varphi$ holds. A formula is true in the model if it has a realizer there, and it is valid if it has a realizer in every model.
examples: In Kleene's number [realizability](c:realizability), a number $e$ realizes $\varphi\to\psi$ when $\{e\}(a)$ is defined and realizes $\psi$ for every realizer $a$ of $\varphi$.
A realizer of $\exists x\,\varphi(x)$ is a pair of a witness $n$ and a realizer of $\varphi(n)$.
Non-example: a realizer is not a truth value; the formula $0=1$ has no realizer in Kleene's model, so it is not true there.

reminder: A computable structure has the natural numbers as its universe, and all its relations and functions are computable.
definition: A [first-order structure](c:structure) is computable (recursive) if its universe is $\mathbb{N}$, or a computable subset of $\mathbb{N}$, and each of its relations is a [computable set](c:computable-set) and each of its functions is a [computable function](c:computable-function) on [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: The standard model $(\mathbb{N},+,\cdot,<)$ of arithmetic is a computable structure.
The ordered field $(\mathbb{Q},+,\cdot,<)$ is computable, when each rational number is coded by a natural number.
Non-example: by Tennenbaum's theorem, no countable nonstandard model of [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) has computable addition and multiplication.

steps: Start with a first-order structure with a countable universe.
Name its elements by natural numbers.
Add the condition that every relation and every function is computable on these names.
links.why: Computability of a structure lets one ask which of its properties an algorithm can decide.

reminder: A group is recursively presented when it has finitely many generators and a recursively enumerable set of defining relations.
definition: A [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group) $G$ is recursively presented if $G\cong\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\mid R\rangle$, where $R$ is a [recursively enumerable set](c:recursively-enumerable-set) of words in the [free group](c:free-group) on $x_1,\dots,x_n$. In other words, an algorithm can list all defining relations, one after the other.
examples: The groups $\mathbb{Z}=\langle x\mid\ \rangle$ and $\mathbb{Z}/n=\langle x\mid x^n\rangle$ are recursively presented.
Every [finitely presented group](c:finitely-presented-group) is recursively presented, because a finite set of relators is recursively enumerable.
Non-example: some two-generator groups are not recursively presented, because there are uncountably many of them up to isomorphism and only countably many recursively enumerable sets of relators.

steps: Take a finitely presented group $\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\mid r_1,\dots,r_m\rangle$.
A finite set of words is a recursively enumerable set.
So the same presentation shows that the group is recursively presented.
links.why: Higman's embedding theorem says that these groups are exactly the finitely generated subgroups of finitely presented groups.

steps: Take a recursively presented group with generators $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
The relators only impose identities between words in these generators.
So the generators still generate the group, and the group is finitely generated, with the added condition that its relators are recursively enumerable.
links.why: The added condition is the one that makes the group fit into the setting of computability.

reminder: Reduced homology is homology changed so that a point has zero homology in every degree.
definition: The reduced homology $\tilde H_n(X)$ of a space $X$ is the [homology](c:homology) of the augmented [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $\cdots\to C_1(X)\to C_0(X)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\mathbb{Z}\to0$, where the [augmentation](c:augmentation) $\varepsilon$ sends each point to $1$. For nonempty $X$, $\tilde H_n(X)=H_n(X)$ when $n>0$, and $H_0(X)\cong\tilde H_0(X)\oplus\mathbb{Z}$.
examples: For a point, $\tilde H_n(\mathrm{pt})=0$ for every $n$.
For the sphere $S^m$, $\tilde H_k(S^m)$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ if $k=m$ and $0$ otherwise.
Non-example: the ordinary homology of a point, $H_0(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{Z}$, is not reduced homology; the reduced homology of a point is zero.

reminder: A reduction is a finite chain of rewrite steps that leads from one term to another.
definition: In an [abstract rewriting system](c:abstract-rewriting-system) $(A,\to)$, a reduction from $a$ to $b$ is a chain $a=a_0\to a_1\to\cdots\to a_n=b$ with $n\ge0$, written $a\twoheadrightarrow b$. The relation $\twoheadrightarrow$ is the reflexive and transitive closure of the [relation](c:relation) $\to$; in the lambda calculus one step is a [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction).
examples: In arithmetic, $(2+3)\cdot4\to5\cdot4\to20$ is a reduction with two steps.
In the lambda calculus, $(\lambda x.\,x\,x)\,y\to y\,y$ is a reduction with one step.
Non-example: going back from $5\cdot4$ to $(2+3)\cdot4$ is not a reduction, because each step must follow a rewrite rule in its forward direction.

reminder: A Lie algebra is reductive when it is the direct sum of a semisimple Lie algebra and an abelian Lie algebra.
definition: A [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ over a field of [characteristic zero](c:char-zero) is reductive if $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{s}\oplus\mathfrak{z}$ is a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of ideals, where $\mathfrak{s}$ is a [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple) and $\mathfrak{z}$ is an [abelian Lie algebra](c:abelian-lie-algebra). Equivalently, the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations.
examples: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is reductive: it is $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb{C})\oplus\mathbb{C}\cdot I$.
Every semisimple Lie algebra and every abelian Lie algebra is reductive.
Non-example: the Lie algebra of upper triangular $2\times2$ matrices is not reductive, because its derived algebra is a nonzero abelian ideal, so it is not semisimple.

steps: Take a semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{s}$.
Take the abelian summand to be zero.
Then $\mathfrak{s}=\mathfrak{s}\oplus0$ is reductive.
links.why: Results about reductive Lie algebras include the semisimple case, with center zero.

steps: Take an abelian Lie algebra $\mathfrak{z}$.
Take the semisimple summand to be zero.
Then $\mathfrak{z}=0\oplus\mathfrak{z}$ is reductive.
links.why: Results about reductive Lie algebras include the abelian case, which has no semisimple part.

reminder: The Rees algebra of an ideal $I$ is the graded ring that has the power $I^n$ in each degree $n$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$. The Rees algebra is the subring $R[It]=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}I^nt^n$ of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[t]$; it is a [graded ring](c:graded-ring) whose degree $n$ part is $I^nt^n$.
examples: For $R=k[x]$ and $I=(x)$, the Rees algebra is $k[x,xt]\subseteq k[x,t]$, a polynomial ring in the two variables $x$ and $xt$.
For $I=R$, every power $I^n$ equals $R$, and the Rees algebra is the polynomial ring $R[t]$.
Non-example: the associated graded ring $\bigoplus_nI^n/I^{n+1}$ is not the Rees algebra, although it is the quotient of the Rees algebra by $I\,R[It]$.

reminder: A regular homotopy is a smooth homotopy $f_t$ in which every map $f_t$ is an immersion.
definition: Let $f_0,f_1:M\to N$ be [immersions](c:immersion) of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold). A regular homotopy from $f_0$ to $f_1$ is a [homotopy](c:homotopy) $f_t$ such that $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) and every $f_t$ is an immersion.
examples: By the Whitney-Graustein theorem, two immersed circles in the plane are regularly homotopic exactly when they have the same rotation number.
By Smale's theorem, the round sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is regularly homotopic to the same sphere turned inside out.
Non-example: the round circle and the figure-eight curve are homotopic, but not regularly homotopic, because their rotation numbers are $1$ and $0$.

steps: Take a smooth homotopy $f_t$ between two smooth maps of manifolds.
Add the condition that every $f_t$ is an immersion.
Such a homotopy is a regular homotopy.
links.why: A regular homotopy keeps the local shape of the map, so it can detect more than a plain homotopy.

reminder: An infinite matrix is regular when it sends every convergent sequence to a sequence with the same limit.
definition: An infinite matrix $A=(a_{nk})$ is regular if, for every sequence $x$ that converges to $L$, the sequence $(Ax)_n=\sum_ka_{nk}x_k$ converges to $L$. By the Silverman-Toeplitz theorem, this holds exactly when three conditions hold: $\sup_n\sum_k|a_{nk}|<\infty$, $a_{nk}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ for each $k$, and $\sum_ka_{nk}\to1$.
examples: The Cesàro matrix with $a_{nk}=1/n$ for $k\le n$ and $a_{nk}=0$ otherwise is regular; it averages the first $n$ terms.
The identity [matrix](c:matrix) is regular.
Non-example: the matrix with $a_{n1}=1$ and all other entries $0$ is not regular; it sends every sequence $x$ to the constant sequence $x_1$.

steps: Define a summation method by $x\mapsto Ax$, the product of a sequence with the matrix.
Regularity of $A$ says that $Ax$ converges to $L$ whenever $x$ converges to $L$.
So the method gives every convergent sequence its ordinary limit, which is the definition of a regular summation method.
links.why: The Silverman-Toeplitz conditions give a test for regularity of every summation method that comes from a matrix.

reminder: The regular representation of a group $G$ is $G$ acting by left multiplication on the vector space with basis $G$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $k$ a field. The regular representation is the [group representation](c:group-representation) on the [vector space](c:vector-space) $k[G]$ with basis $\{e_g\}_{g\in G}$, where $h\cdot e_g=e_{hg}$; it is the linearization of the action of $G$ on itself by left multiplication, a [permutation representation](c:permutation-representation). More generally, an [associative unital algebra](c:associative-unital-algebra) acts on itself by left multiplication.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ over $\mathbb{C}$, the regular representation has dimension 2 and splits into the trivial and the sign representation.
For a finite group $G$ over $\mathbb{C}$, each irreducible representation $V$ occurs $\dim V$ times in the regular representation.
Non-example: the trivial representation on $k$ is not the regular representation of a group with more than one element, because its dimension is $1$ and not $|G|$.

steps: Let $G$ act on the set $G$ by left multiplication.
Take the vector space with basis $G$, and extend the action linearly.
The result is a particular representation of $G$ that contains every irreducible representation of a finite group.
links.why: Every statement about all group representations applies to the regular representation, which is the universal test case.

steps: Take the set $G$ with the action of $G$ by left multiplication.
Form the vector space with this set as a basis.
This permutation representation is the regular representation.
links.why: It shows that the regular representation is the permutation representation of the simplest free transitive action.

reminder: The regulator of a number field is the covolume of its units modulo torsion in the logarithmic embedding.
definition: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with $r_1$ real and $r_2$ complex places, let $r=r_1+r_2-1$, and choose [fundamental units](c:fundamental-unit) $u_1,\dots,u_r$ of the [unit group](c:unit-group) modulo torsion. The regulator $R_K$ is the absolute value of the [determinant](c:determinant) of the matrix with entries $\delta_i\log|u_j|_i$, built from any $r$ of the $r+1$ places, where $\delta_i=1$ at a real place and $\delta_i=2$ at a complex place. Here $\log$ is the real [logarithm](c:logarithm).
examples: For $\mathbb{Q}$ and for imaginary quadratic fields, the unit group is finite, so $r=0$ and the regulator is $1$.
For $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, the fundamental unit is $1+\sqrt2$, so $R=\log(1+\sqrt2)\approx0.881$.
Non-example: the number $\log|u|$ of a unit $u$ that is not fundamental is not the regulator; for $u=(1+\sqrt2)^2$ it equals $2R$.

reminder: The regulator of a number field is a positive real number that measures the size of its group of units.
definition: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) $\mathcal{O}_K$, with $r_1$ real and $r_2$ complex places, and let $r=r_1+r_2-1$. The map $u\mapsto(\delta_i\log|u|_i)_i$, with $\delta_i=1$ at a real place and $2$ at a complex place, sends the [group of units](c:group-of-units) $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ onto a lattice of rank $r$ in the hyperplane where the coordinates sum to $0$. The regulator $R_K$ is the covolume of this lattice, which is the absolute value of the [determinant](c:determinant) of the matrix of [logarithms](c:logarithm) that remains after deleting one row.
examples: For $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, the unit group is finite, so the lattice is $\{0\}$ and $R_K=1$.
For $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$, the fundamental unit is $(1+\sqrt5)/2$, so $R_K=\log\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx0.481$.
Non-example: the class number $h_K$ is not the regulator; $h_K$ counts ideal classes, and $R_K$ measures units.

reminder: A Reinhardt cardinal is the critical point of a non-trivial elementary embedding of the universe of sets into itself.
definition: A Reinhardt cardinal is the critical point of a non-trivial [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $j:V\to V$ of the universe of sets into itself, that is, the least ordinal $\kappa$ with $j(\kappa)\neq\kappa$. Kunen's inconsistency theorem shows that no such $j$ exists in [ZFC](c:zfc), so one studies it in ZF without the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice). Because $j$ is a class, the statement is formalized in ZF with an extra function symbol for $j$.
examples: In ZF plus an elementary embedding $j:V\to V$, the critical point $\kappa$ of $j$ is a Reinhardt cardinal.
The sets $X\subseteq\kappa$ with $\kappa\in j(X)$ form a $\kappa$-complete ultrafilter on $\kappa$, so a Reinhardt cardinal is measurable.
Non-example: a measurable cardinal gives an embedding $j:V\to M$ into a proper inner model $M\neq V$; this does not make the cardinal Reinhardt.

steps: Large cardinal axioms often say that a cardinal is the critical point of an elementary embedding.
For a measurable cardinal, the embedding goes from $V$ into an inner model $M$.
For a Reinhardt cardinal, the target is $V$ itself, which is the extreme case that Kunen's theorem rules out in ZFC.
links.why: It shows where Reinhardt cardinals sit among the large cardinal axioms that come from elementary embeddings.

reminder: Relational algebra builds new finite relations from given ones by selection, projection, union, difference, product and renaming.
definition: Relational algebra is a set of operations on finite [relations](c:relation), each seen as a table with named attributes. The basic operations are selection, projection, union, set difference, [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) and renaming. A query is an expression that combines these operations, and its value is a new finite relation.
examples: Selection $\sigma_{\mathrm{age}>30}(R)$ keeps the tuples of $R$ whose age is above 30.
Projection $\pi_{\mathrm{name}}(R)$ keeps only the name column of $R$ and removes duplicate rows.
The natural join of $R$ and $S$ is derived: it is a product, followed by a selection and a projection.
Non-example: the transitive closure of a relation is not expressible in relational algebra, because it needs recursion.

reminder: A relational calculus query names the wanted tuples by a first-order formula, not by a sequence of operations.
definition: Relational calculus is a declarative query language on finite [relations](c:relation). A query $\{(x_1,\dots,x_k)\mid\varphi\}$ returns all tuples that satisfy the [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula $\varphi$ whose atoms are the stored relations. By Codd's theorem, the domain independent queries of this language are exactly the queries of [relational algebra](c:relational-algebra).
examples: The query $\{x\mid\exists y\,\mathrm{Parent}(x,y)\}$ returns every $x$ that is the parent of someone.
The query $\{(x,z)\mid\exists y\,(R(x,y)\wedge S(y,z))\}$ returns the composition of the relations $R$ and $S$.
Non-example: $\{x\mid\neg R(x)\}$ is not domain independent; its answer is every value outside $R$, so it depends on the whole domain.

reminder: The relative cohomology $H^n(X,A)$ is the cohomology of the cochains on $X$ that vanish on the subspace $A$.
definition: For a space $X$ and a subspace $A\subseteq X$, the relative cochain complex consists of the [cochains](c:cochain) on $X$ whose restriction to $A$ is zero. The relative cohomology $H^n(X,A)$ is the [cohomology](c:cohomology) of this [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex). It fits into the [long exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $\cdots\to H^n(X,A)\to H^n(X)\to H^n(A)\to H^{n+1}(X,A)\to\cdots$.
examples: For the pair $(D^n,S^{n-1})$ of a disk and its boundary sphere, $H^k(D^n,S^{n-1})$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ if $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For a point $p$ in $X$, $H^n(X,\{p\})$ is the reduced cohomology $\tilde H^n(X)$.
Non-example: the cohomology $H^n(A)$ of the subspace alone is not $H^n(X,A)$; the relative groups also see how $A$ sits in $X$.

steps: Take the subspace $A$ to be empty.
Then every cochain on $X$ vanishes on $A$ without any condition.
So the relative cochain complex is the ordinary one, and $H^n(X,\emptyset)=H^n(X)$.
links.why: Ordinary cohomology is the special case in which the relative condition is empty.

reminder: A subset of a space is relatively compact when its closure in the space is compact.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $S$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is relatively compact if its [closure](c:closure) in $X$ is [compact](c:compact-subspace). In a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space), this holds exactly when $S$ lies in some compact subset.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, a set is relatively compact exactly when it is bounded.
The open interval $(0,1)$ is relatively compact in $\mathbb{R}$, because its closure $[0,1]$ is compact.
Non-example: in the space $X=(0,2)$, the subset $(0,1)$ is not relatively compact, because its closure $(0,1]$ in $X$ is not compact.

steps: Take a compact subset $K$ of a Hausdorff space $X$.
A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed, so the closure of $K$ is $K$.
So the closure of $K$ is compact, and $K$ is relatively compact.
links.why: Relative compactness keeps the useful finiteness of compact sets while allowing sets that are not closed.

reminder: The representation ring $R(G)$ is the ring of virtual representations of $G$, with direct sum as addition and tensor product as multiplication.
definition: For a [group](c:group) $G$, the representation ring $R(G)$ is the [Grothendieck ring](c:grothendieck-ring) of the category of finite-dimensional complex [representations](c:group-representation) of $G$. Its elements are formal differences of representations; addition comes from the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) and multiplication comes from the tensor product.
examples: For the trivial group, $R(G)=\mathbb{Z}$.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}/n$, $R(G)\cong\mathbb{Z}[t]/(t^n-1)$, where $t$ is a faithful one-dimensional representation.
For a finite group, $R(G)$ is a free abelian group with the irreducible representations as a basis.
Non-example: the group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ is not $R(G)$; it is one representation, the regular one, and not a ring of classes of representations.

reminder: A resolution of an object $X$ is a weak equivalence between $X$ and a better-behaved object.
definition: In a category with [weak equivalences](c:weak-equivalence), a resolution of an [object](c:object) $X$ is an object $X'$ with a weak equivalence $X'\to X$, or $X\to X'$, where $X'$ has a useful property such as being cofibrant or fibrant. In homological algebra, a resolution of a module $M$ is an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to M\to0$ in which each $P_i$ is projective, or injective in the dual case.
examples: The sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/n\to0$ is a free resolution of the abelian group $\mathbb{Z}/n$.
A [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $\Gamma X$ with a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) $\Gamma X\to X$ is a resolution of the space $X$.
Non-example: the inclusion of a point into a circle is not a weak equivalence, so a point is not a resolution of a circle.

reminder: The restriction of a function to a subset uses the same rule but takes only the inputs from that subset.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [function](c:function) and $U\subseteq X$ a [subset](c:subset). The restriction $f|_U:U\to Y$ is the [composition](c:composition) of $f$ with the [inclusion function](c:inclusion-function) $U\hookrightarrow X$, so $f|_U(u)=f(u)$ for every $u\in U$.
examples: The restriction of $x\mapsto x^2$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $[0,\infty)$ is injective, but the function on $\mathbb{R}$ is not.
The restriction of a continuous function to a subspace is continuous.
Non-example: a function on a larger set that agrees with $f$ on $U$ is an extension of $f|_U$; it is not a restriction of $f$ to $U$, because its domain is larger than $U$.

reminder: A ribbon graph is a graph with a cyclic order on the half-edges at each vertex.
definition: A ribbon graph (or fat graph) is a [graph](c:graph) with a [cyclic order](c:cyclic-order) on the set of half-edges at each vertex. In formal terms, it is a set $H$ of half-edges with a fixed-point-free [involution](c:involution) $\iota$ (its orbits are the edges) and a permutation $\sigma$ (its [cycles](c:cycle) are the vertices with their cyclic orders). The cycles of $\sigma\iota$ are the boundary components of the [surface](c:surface) that one gets by thickening the graph into ribbons.
examples: A graph drawn in the plane, with the cyclic order read counterclockwise at each vertex, is a ribbon graph that thickens to a planar surface.
One vertex with one loop is a ribbon graph that thickens to an annulus.
One vertex with two loops, with the half-edges in the order $a,b,a',b'$, thickens to a torus with one hole.
Non-example: a graph with a vertex of degree 3 or more and no chosen cyclic order is not yet a ribbon graph, because different orders give different surfaces.

steps: Forget the cyclic orders of a ribbon graph.
What remains is the underlying graph, with the same vertices and edges.
So a ribbon graph is a graph with one more structure, a cyclic order of the half-edges at each vertex.
links.why: The extra cyclic order turns a combinatorial graph into a description of a surface.

reminder: A Riemann-Hilbert problem asks for an object, such as a differential equation or a function, with prescribed monodromy or jumps.
definition: In its classical form, one is given points $a_1,\dots,a_n$ of the Riemann sphere and a [representation](c:group-representation) of the fundamental group of their complement, and one looks for a linear [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) with [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) coefficients whose [monodromy](c:monodromy) is this representation. In the contour form, one looks for a matrix function that is holomorphic off a contour, has a prescribed jump across the contour, and has a fixed value at infinity.
examples: For three points $0,1,\infty$ and an irreducible rank 2 monodromy representation, Riemann's solution is a hypergeometric equation.
Splitting a matrix function on a circle as a product of a function holomorphic outside the circle and a function holomorphic inside is a Riemann-Hilbert problem.
Non-example: solving a given differential equation for its solutions is not a Riemann-Hilbert problem; the problem runs the other way, from the monodromy to an equation.

reminder: A Riemann sum approximates the integral of a function by a sum of rectangle areas over a partition of the interval.
definition: Let $f$ be a [function](c:function) on a closed [interval](c:interval) $[a,b]$, let $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$ be a partition, and let $t_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ be sample points. The Riemann sum is $\sum_{i=1}^nf(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$; if these sums converge to one number as the mesh $\max_i(x_i-x_{i-1})$ tends to $0$, this number is the [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) of $f$.
examples: For $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ with $n$ equal pieces and left end points, the sum is $\frac{n-1}{2n}$, which tends to $\frac12$.
The left, right and midpoint rules are Riemann sums with special choices of the sample points $t_i$.
Non-example: the sum $\sum_if(x_i)$ without the widths $x_i-x_{i-1}$ is not a Riemann sum; it grows without bound when the partition is refined.

reminder: A ring isomorphism is a bijection between two rings that preserves addition and multiplication.
definition: A ring isomorphism $f:R\to S$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) that is also a [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism): $f(a+b)=f(a)+f(b)$ and $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$ for all $a,b\in R$, and $f(1)=1$ for rings with a unit. Equivalently, $f$ is a ring homomorphism that has an inverse map that is also a ring homomorphism.
examples: Complex conjugation $z\mapsto\bar z$ is a ring isomorphism from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{C}$.
The Chinese remainder theorem gives a ring isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\times\mathbb{Z}/3$.
Non-example: the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is an injective ring homomorphism, but it is not a ring isomorphism, because it is not surjective.

steps: Take a ring homomorphism $f:R\to S$.
Add the condition that $f$ is a bijection.
The inverse map of $f$ is then also a ring homomorphism, so $f$ is a ring isomorphism.
links.why: A ring isomorphism lets one move every ring-theoretic statement from $R$ to $S$ without loss.

steps: Work in the category whose objects are rings and whose morphisms are ring homomorphisms.
An isomorphism there is a morphism $f$ with an inverse morphism $g$.
Such an $f$ is exactly a bijective ring homomorphism, because the inverse of a bijective homomorphism is a homomorphism.
links.why: It shows that the general notion of isomorphism, in the category of rings, is the familiar bijective homomorphism.

reminder: The ring $C(X)$ has all continuous real functions on $X$ as elements, with pointwise addition and multiplication.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$, the ring $C(X)$ is the set of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) $X\to\mathbb{R}$, with $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ and $(fg)(x)=f(x)g(x)$. It is a commutative [ring](c:ring) whose unit is the constant function $1$, and it is an algebra over the [real numbers](c:real-number).
examples: For a one-point space $X$, $C(X)\cong\mathbb{R}$; for a discrete space with $n$ points, $C(X)\cong\mathbb{R}^n$.
For $X=[0,1]$, the ring $C(X)$ has zero divisors: if $f$ vanishes on $[\tfrac12,1]$ and $g$ vanishes on $[0,\tfrac12]$, then $fg=0$.
Non-example: the continuous functions of compact support on $\mathbb{R}$ are closed under addition and multiplication, but they have no unit, so they do not form $C(\mathbb{R})$.

reminder: In a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of functions, point evaluation is a continuous linear functional.
definition: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space on a set $X$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ of [functions](c:function) $X\to\mathbb{C}$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the [evaluation map](c:evaluation-map) $f\mapsto f(x)$ is a continuous linear functional on $H$. By the Riesz representation theorem, each $x$ then has a vector $k_x\in H$ with $f(x)=\langle f,k_x\rangle$ for all $f\in H$, and $k(x,y)=\langle k_y,k_x\rangle$ is the reproducing kernel.
examples: The Hardy space $H^2$ of the unit disk is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with the Szegő kernel $k(z,w)=1/(1-z\bar w)$.
The Paley-Wiener space of band-limited functions with the $L^2$ norm is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a sinc kernel.
Non-example: $L^2[0,1]$ is not a reproducing kernel Hilbert space; its elements are classes of functions, so evaluation at a point is not even defined.

steps: Take a Hilbert space $H$ whose elements are functions on a set $X$.
Add the condition that each evaluation $f\mapsto f(x)$ is continuous.
By the Riesz representation theorem, each evaluation is an inner product with a vector, and these vectors give the kernel.
links.why: The condition gives a kernel $k(x,y)$ that encodes the whole space, which is the basis of kernel methods.

reminder: The $n$th roots of unity are the complex numbers $z$ with $z^n=1$.
definition: For a positive integer $n$, the $n$th roots of unity are the [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $x^n-1$ in the [complex numbers](c:complex-number); they are $e^{2\pi ik/n}$ for $k=0,\dots,n-1$. They form a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) of order $n$ under multiplication.
examples: The 4th roots of unity are $1$, $i$, $-1$ and $-i$.
The cube roots of unity are $1$ and $\frac{-1\pm i\sqrt3}{2}$.
Non-example: the number $2$ is not a root of unity, because $2^n\neq1$ for every positive integer $n$.

steps: Take a primitive $n$th root of unity $\zeta$, a root whose order is exactly $n$.
Each power $\zeta^k$ satisfies $(\zeta^k)^n=1$.
The $n$ powers $\zeta^0,\dots,\zeta^{n-1}$ are then all the $n$th roots of unity, and the primitive ones are those with order exactly $n$.
links.why: It shows that the $n$th roots of unity are the powers of one primitive root.

reminder: A rotation turns every point of the plane by the same angle about a fixed center and keeps all distances.
definition: A rotation of the Euclidean plane about a point $c$ by an angle $\theta$ is the map $x\mapsto c+R_\theta(x-c)$, where $R_\theta$ is the matrix of a turn by $\theta$; it is an [isometry](c:isometry) that preserves orientation and has the center $c$ as its only [fixed point](c:fixed-point), unless it is the identity. In [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$, a rotation about the origin is a linear map given by an element of the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group).
examples: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ is the rotation of the plane by $90^\circ$ about the origin.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$, a rotation about an axis fixes every point of the axis and turns each plane perpendicular to the axis.
Non-example: a reflection in a line is an isometry, but it reverses orientation and fixes a whole line, so it is not a rotation.

steps: Take a rotation $\rho$ about a point $c$ of the plane.
It keeps the distance between any two points, so it is an isometry.
Add the conditions that $\rho$ preserves orientation and has $c$ as its only fixed point, or is the identity.
links.why: Every fact about isometries applies to rotations, and the added conditions single out the rotations among them.

reminder: A function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is rotation invariant when $f(\rho x)=f(x)$ for every rotation $\rho$ about the origin.
definition: An object on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is rotation invariant if every [rotation](c:rotation) about the origin leaves it unchanged. For a [function](c:function) $f$ this means $f(\rho x)=f(x)$ for all $\rho$ in the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group); for a random vector $X$ it means that $\rho X$ has the same distribution as $X$.
examples: The function $f(x)=\|x\|^2$ is rotation invariant, and a function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge2$ is rotation invariant exactly when it depends only on $\|x\|$.
The standard Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with density proportional to $e^{-\|x\|^2/2}$, is rotation invariant.
Non-example: $f(x,y)=x$ is not rotation invariant, because a quarter turn sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$ and changes the value from $1$ to $0$.

reminder: A model of cardinality $\kappa$ is saturated when it realizes every type over fewer than $\kappa$ parameters.
definition: A [model](c:model) $M$ is $\kappa$-saturated if, for every [subset](c:subset) $A\subseteq M$ with fewer than $\kappa$ elements, every [complete type](c:complete-type) in one variable over $A$ is realized by an element of $M$. It is saturated if it is $\kappa$-saturated for $\kappa$ equal to its own [cardinal number](c:cardinal-number).
examples: The countable dense linear order $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ without end points is saturated.
Every finite structure is saturated.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{R},<)$ is not saturated, because the type $\{x>n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ over the countable set $\mathbb{N}$ is not realized in $\mathbb{R}$.

reminder: The Schur functor of a partition $\lambda$ of $n$ sends a vector space $V$ to the $\lambda$-part of $V^{\otimes n}$.
definition: Work over a field of [characteristic zero](c:char-zero). Let $\lambda$ be an [integer partition](c:integer-partition) of $n$, and let $S^\lambda$ be the irreducible representation of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $\Sigma_n$ that it labels. The Schur functor $\mathbb{S}_\lambda$ is the [functor](c:functor) that sends a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Sigma_n}(S^\lambda,V^{\otimes n})$, where $\Sigma_n$ permutes the tensor factors.
examples: For $\lambda=(n)$, $\mathbb{S}_\lambda(V)$ is the symmetric power $\operatorname{Sym}^nV$; for $\lambda=(1^n)$, it is the exterior power $\Lambda^nV$.
For $\lambda=(2,1)$ and $\dim V=2$, $\mathbb{S}_\lambda(V)$ has dimension $2$.
Non-example: the functor $V\mapsto V^{\otimes n}$ is not a single Schur functor; by Schur-Weyl duality it is a sum of the Schur functors $\mathbb{S}_\lambda$, each repeated $\dim S^\lambda$ times.

reminder: The Schur polynomial $s_\lambda$ is the sum of the monomials $x^T$ over all semistandard Young tableaux $T$ of shape $\lambda$.
definition: For an [integer partition](c:integer-partition) $\lambda$ and variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, the Schur polynomial is $s_\lambda=\sum_Tx^T$, where $T$ runs over the [semistandard Young tableaux](c:semistandard-young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$ with entries in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $x^T=\prod_ix_i^{\#\{i\text{ in }T\}}$. Equivalently, it is a quotient of two alternants, $s_\lambda=\det(x_j^{\lambda_i+n-i})/\det(x_j^{n-i})$, and it is a [symmetric polynomial](c:symmetric-polynomial).
examples: For $\lambda=(1)$, $s_\lambda=x_1+\cdots+x_n$; for $\lambda=(1^k)$ it is the elementary symmetric polynomial $e_k$.
In two variables, $s_{(2,1)}(x,y)=x^2y+xy^2$.
Non-example: the monomial symmetric polynomial $m_{(2,1)}$ is not the Schur polynomial $s_{(2,1)}$; in three variables, $s_{(2,1)}=m_{(2,1)}+2m_{(1,1,1)}$.

steps: Take the Schur polynomial $s_\lambda$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$.
Swapping two variables swaps two columns of the numerator determinant and of the denominator determinant, so the quotient is unchanged.
Hence $s_\lambda$ is a symmetric polynomial, with the extra property that its coefficients in the monomial basis are non-negative integers.
links.why: Schur polynomials form a basis of the symmetric polynomials, so every symmetric polynomial is a combination of them.

reminder: The Schwarzschild metric is the spherically symmetric vacuum solution of Einstein's equations outside a non-rotating mass.
definition: In geometric units, the Schwarzschild metric of mass $M$ is the [Lorentzian metric](c:lorentzian-manifold) $ds^2=-\left(1-\tfrac{2M}{r}\right)dt^2+\left(1-\tfrac{2M}{r}\right)^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$ on the region $r>2M$. It is spherically symmetric, and it solves the vacuum [Einstein equation](c:einstein-equation), which says that the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) is zero.
examples: For $M=0$, the metric is the flat Minkowski metric.
For $M>0$, it models the gravitational field outside a static spherical body, such as a star, in general relativity.
Non-example: the Kerr metric is also a vacuum solution, but it is not the Schwarzschild metric; it describes a rotating mass and is not spherically symmetric.

reminder: A function between dcpos is Scott continuous when it preserves the supremum of every directed set.
definition: A function $f:P\to Q$ between [directed-complete partial orders](c:dcpo) is Scott continuous if $f(\sup D)=\sup f(D)$ for every directed subset $D\subseteq P$. Such a function is automatically [monotone](c:monotone-function), and the supremum is the [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound).
examples: On the chain $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$, the function with $f(n)=n+1$ and $f(\infty)=\infty$ is Scott continuous.
Every monotone function between finite posets is Scott continuous, because every finite directed set has a greatest element.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$, the function with $f(n)=0$ and $f(\infty)=1$ is monotone but not Scott continuous, because $\sup f(\mathbb{N})=0$ while $f(\sup\mathbb{N})=1$.

steps: Take a Scott continuous function $f$ and two elements $a\le b$.
The set $\{a,b\}$ is directed and its supremum is $b$.
So $f(b)$ equals the supremum of $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, which gives $f(a)\le f(b)$ and shows that $f$ is monotone.
Conversely, a monotone map is Scott continuous when it also preserves the suprema of all directed sets.
links.why: Scott continuity is the monotone case that also respects limits of directed sets, which Kleene's fixed-point theorem needs.

reminder: A second-order linear ODE has the form $a(x)y''+b(x)y'+c(x)y=f(x)$ for an unknown function $y$.
definition: A second-order linear [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) is an equation $a(x)y''+b(x)y'+c(x)y=f(x)$ for an unknown function $y(x)$, where $a$ is not identically zero. It is homogeneous when $f=0$; then its solutions on an interval, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are continuous and $a\neq0$, form a two-dimensional [vector space](c:vector-space).
examples: The equation $y''+y=0$ has the solutions $y=A\cos x+B\sin x$.
Bessel's equation $x^2y''+xy'+(x^2-\nu^2)y=0$ is a second-order linear ODE.
Non-example: $y''+y^2=0$ has order two, but it is not linear, because $y^2$ is not a linear function of $y$.

steps: Take a linear differential equation for one unknown function $y$ of one variable.
Restrict to equations whose highest derivative of $y$ is the second derivative.
The equation then has the form $a(x)y''+b(x)y'+c(x)y=f(x)$.
links.why: Results on linear equations, such as the superposition principle, apply to every second-order equation of this form.

reminder: The Seiberg-Witten equations couple a $U(1)$ connection and a spinor by a Dirac equation and a curvature equation.
definition: On a closed oriented [Riemannian 4-manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) with a $\mathrm{spin}^c$ structure, the unknowns are a connection $A$ on a [principal U(1)-bundle](c:principal-u-1-bundle) and a section $\psi$ of a [spinor bundle](c:spinor-bundle). The equations are $D_A\psi=0$ and $F_A^+=q(\psi)$, where $D_A$ is the Dirac operator, $F_A^+$ is the self-dual part of the [curvature](c:curvature), and $q(\psi)$ is quadratic in $\psi$. Gauge equivalence classes of solutions form a [moduli space](c:moduli-space) that defines the Seiberg-Witten invariants.
examples: A solution with $\psi=0$ is called reducible; then the equations reduce to $F_A^+=0$.
On a closed 4-manifold with a metric of positive scalar curvature, every solution is reducible, by a Weitzenböck formula.
Non-example: the equation $D_A\psi=0$ alone is the linear Dirac equation; it is not the Seiberg-Witten system, because the coupling $F_A^+=q(\psi)$ is missing.

reminder: A Seifert fibration writes a 3-manifold as a circle bundle over a 2-dimensional orbifold.
definition: A Seifert fibration of a [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$ is a map $M\to B$ to a 2-dimensional [orbifold](c:orbifold) that is a [circle bundle](c:circle-bundle) in the orbifold sense. Away from the cone points of $B$ it is an ordinary [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle) with fibre $S^1$; over a cone point of order $p$ the fibre is exceptional, and it has a neighbourhood that is a fibred solid torus.
examples: The product $S^2\times S^1$ has a Seifert fibration over $S^2$ with no exceptional fibres.
The Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ is a Seifert fibration with no exceptional fibres.
The Poincaré homology sphere has a Seifert fibration over $S^2$ with three exceptional fibres, of orders $2$, $3$ and $5$.
Non-example: a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold has no Seifert fibration.

steps: Take a circle bundle $M\to B$ over a closed surface $B$.
Regard $B$ as an orbifold with no cone points.
Then $M\to B$ is a Seifert fibration with no exceptional fibres.
links.why: Seifert fibrations add the exceptional fibres, which makes all the standard models of 3-manifolds with circle symmetry fit.

reminder: A Selmer group is the subgroup of a Galois cohomology group of classes that satisfy a local condition at every place.
definition: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) and $M$ a [Galois representation](c:galois-representation) of its [absolute Galois group](c:absolute-galois-group). Give a subgroup $L_v$ of the local cohomology group $H^1(K_v,M)$ for each place $v$; the Selmer group is the set of classes in the first [Galois cohomology](c:galois-cohomology) group $H^1(K,M)$ whose restriction to $K_v$ lies in $L_v$ for all $v$. For an elliptic curve $E$ and $M=E[n]$, the $L_v$ are the images of $E(K_v)/nE(K_v)$.
examples: For an elliptic curve $E$ over $K$, the $n$-Selmer group $\mathrm{Sel}^{(n)}(E/K)$ is finite, and it contains $E(K)/nE(K)$.
The Selmer group sits in an exact sequence $0\to E(K)/nE(K)\to\mathrm{Sel}^{(n)}(E/K)\to\text{Sha}(E/K)[n]\to0$.
Non-example: the whole group $H^1(K,E[n])$ is not a Selmer group; it has no local conditions and is infinite.

reminder: The semidirect product $\mathfrak{g}\ltimes\mathfrak{a}$ is the vector space $\mathfrak{g}\oplus\mathfrak{a}$ with a bracket that uses an action of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $\mathfrak{a}$.
definition: Let a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ act on a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{a}$ by [derivations](c:derivation-lie-algebra), that is, by a Lie algebra homomorphism $\phi:\mathfrak{g}\to\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak{a})$ (a [Lie algebra action](c:lie-algebra-action)). The semidirect product $\mathfrak{g}\ltimes\mathfrak{a}$ is the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [vector spaces](c:vector-space) $\mathfrak{g}\oplus\mathfrak{a}$ with the bracket $[(x,a),(y,b)]=([x,y],\ \phi(x)b-\phi(y)a+[a,b])$.
examples: The Euclidean Lie algebra $\mathfrak{e}(n)=\mathfrak{so}(n)\ltimes\mathbb{R}^n$ is the Lie algebra of the isometries of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The Poincaré Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)\ltimes\mathbb{R}^4$, with $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^4$ in the usual way.

Non-example: the simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is not a semidirect product of two nonzero Lie algebras, because $\mathfrak{a}$ is always an ideal and $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ has no proper nonzero ideal.

steps: Take two Lie algebras $\mathfrak{g}$ and $\mathfrak{a}$ and the zero action $\phi=0$.
Then the bracket becomes $[(x,a),(y,b)]=([x,y],[a,b])$.
This is the bracket of the direct product, so the direct product is the semidirect product with trivial action.
links.why: The semidirect product lets the two factors interact, and the direct product is the case where they do not.

reminder: A semigroup is a set with an associative binary operation.
definition: A semigroup is a [set](c:set) $S$ with a binary operation $(a,b)\mapsto ab$ that is [associative](c:associativity), that is, $(ab)c=a(bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in S$. The operation need not have an [identity element](c:identity-element).
examples: The positive integers under addition form a semigroup without an identity element.
The set of all functions from a set $X$ to itself, under composition, is a semigroup.
Non-example: the integers under subtraction are not a semigroup, because $(1-2)-3=-4$ but $1-(2-3)=2$.

steps: Take a monoid $(M,\cdot,1)$.
Forget the identity element $1$.
What remains is an associative operation on $M$, so $M$ is a semigroup.
links.why: Every monoid is a semigroup, so facts about semigroups apply to monoids, groups and many other structures.

steps: Take a magma, a set with a binary operation.
Add the condition that the operation is associative.
The result is a semigroup.
links.why: Associativity is the one condition that separates semigroups from general magmas.

reminder: Every module over a semisimple ring is a direct sum of simple modules.
definition: A ring $R$ is semisimple if it is [Artinian](c:artinian-ring) and its [Jacobson radical](c:jacobson-radical) is zero. Equivalently, $R$ is a finite direct sum of simple left ideals, or every left [module](c:module) over $R$ is a [semisimple module](c:is-semisimple-module).
examples: Every field and every division ring is semisimple.
The matrix ring $M_n(k)$ over a field $k$ is semisimple.
The group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$ of a finite group $G$ is semisimple, by Maschke's theorem.
Non-example: the ring $k[x]/(x^2)$ is Artinian, but its Jacobson radical $(x)$ is not zero, so it is not semisimple.

steps: Take an Artinian ring $R$.
Add the condition that its Jacobson radical is zero.
Then every module over $R$ is semisimple, so $R$ is a semisimple ring.
links.why: The Artin-Wedderburn theorem describes exactly these Artinian rings, as products of matrix rings over division rings.

reminder: A sequence coding assigns to each finite sequence of natural numbers a single natural number from which one can decode the sequence.
definition: A sequence coding is a map that sends each finite [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number) to a code number, so that the length and each entry can be recovered from the code by a [computable function](c:computable-function). Gödel's beta function gives such a coding in arithmetic: with $\beta(c,d,i)=c\bmod(1+(i+1)d)$, every finite sequence $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}$ has numbers $c,d$ with $\beta(c,d,i)=a_i$ for all $i<n$.
examples: The prime power coding sends $(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})$ to $p_0^{a_0+1}\cdots p_{n-1}^{a_{n-1}+1}$, where $p_i$ is the $i$th prime.
Gödel's beta function codes any finite sequence by two numbers $c$ and $d$, and uses only addition and multiplication.
Non-example: the sum $a_0+\cdots+a_{n-1}$ is not a coding, because the sequences $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ have the same sum, so one cannot decode.

reminder: A sequent $\Gamma\vdash\Delta$ is a formal statement that the formulas $\Gamma$ entail the formulas $\Delta$.
definition: A sequent is an expression $\Gamma\vdash\Delta$ of the [metalanguage](c:metalanguage), where the [antecedent](c:antecedent) $\Gamma$ is a list of formulas that forms a [context](c:context) of hypotheses, and the [consequent](c:consequent) $\Delta$ is a list of formulas. It means that, if all formulas of $\Gamma$ hold, then some formula of $\Delta$ holds; in intuitionistic and type-theoretic systems, $\Delta$ is one formula or one judgment.
examples: The sequent $A,B\vdash A\wedge B$ is derivable: from $A$ and $B$ one gets $A\wedge B$.
The sequent $\vdash A\vee\neg A$ has an empty antecedent and is derivable in classical logic.
In type theory, $x:\mathbb{N}\vdash x+1:\mathbb{N}$ is a typing judgment in sequent form.
Non-example: the formula $A\to B$ is not a sequent; it is a statement of the object language, while $A\vdash B$ is a statement about derivability in the metalanguage.

steps: Start with a plain judgment, such as 'A is true'.
Add a list of hypotheses $\Gamma$ under which the judgment is made.
The result, written $\Gamma\vdash A$, is a hypothetical judgment, and it is a sequent.
links.why: It shows that a sequent is a judgment that depends on a context, so its rules are the rules of reasoning from hypotheses.

reminder: A Serre functor $S$ gives natural isomorphisms $\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(B,S(A))^*$ for all objects $A$ and $B$.
definition: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a Hom-finite $k$-linear [triangulated category](c:triangulated-category). A Serre functor is an [exact functor](c:exact-functor) $S:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}$ with [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism) $\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(B,S(A))^*$ for all objects $A,B$, where ${}^*$ is the [dual space](c:dual-space).
examples: For a smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$, the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves has the Serre functor $S=-\otimes\omega_X[n]$, which is Serre duality.
For a finite-dimensional algebra $A$ of finite global dimension, the bounded derived category of finite-dimensional modules has the Serre functor $S=-\otimes^L_AD(A)$.
Non-example: the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on the affine line $\mathbb{A}^1$ has no Serre functor, because $\mathbb{A}^1$ is not proper.

reminder: The Serre spectral sequence computes the homology of the total space of a fibration from the homology of its base and fibre.
definition: For a [fibration](c:fibration) $F\to E\to B$ over a path-connected base $B$, the Serre spectral sequence is a [spectral sequence](c:spectral-sequence) with second page $E^2_{p,q}=H_p(B;H_q(F))$ that converges to the [homology](c:homology) $H_{p+q}(E)$. The coefficients $H_q(F)$ form a local system on $B$, which is trivial when $B$ is simply connected. The version for [cohomology](c:cohomology) has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(B;H^q(F))\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(E)$.
examples: For the Hopf fibration $S^1\to S^3\to S^2$, the differential $d_2:E^2_{2,0}\to E^2_{0,1}$ is an isomorphism, and the class in $E^2_{2,1}$ gives $H_3(S^3)=\mathbb{Z}$.
For a product $B\times F$ with field coefficients, the sequence collapses at the second page and recovers the Künneth formula.
Non-example: the map $\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$, $x\mapsto x^2$, is not a fibration, because its fibre is one point over $0$ and two points over every positive number.

reminder: A sesquilinear form is linear in one argument and conjugate-linear in the other.
definition: On a complex [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$, a sesquilinear form is a function $B:V\times V\to\mathbb{C}$ that is linear in the second argument and [conjugate-linear](c:antilinear-map) in the first: $B(\lambda u+\mu v,w)=\bar\lambda B(u,w)+\bar\mu B(v,w)$ and $B(u,\lambda v+\mu w)=\lambda B(u,v)+\mu B(u,w)$ for [complex numbers](c:complex-number) $\lambda,\mu$. Some authors swap the two arguments.
examples: The standard inner product $B(u,v)=\sum_i\bar u_iv_i$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is a sesquilinear form.
For every complex matrix $A$, the form $B(u,v)=u^*Av$ is sesquilinear.
Non-example: $B(u,v)=\sum_iu_iv_i$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is bilinear, but it is not sesquilinear, because scaling $u$ by $i$ multiplies $B$ by $i$ and not by $-i$.

steps: Take a bilinear form $B$ on a real vector space.
For a real scalar $\lambda$, the conjugate $\bar\lambda$ equals $\lambda$.
So $B$ is linear in both arguments in the sesquilinear sense, and a real bilinear form is a sesquilinear form with trivial conjugation.
links.why: Sesquilinear forms are the complex counterpart of bilinear forms, and they give inner products and Hermitian forms.

reminder: A shift space is a closed set of bi-infinite sequences over a finite alphabet that is invariant under the shift.
definition: Let $A$ be a [finite set](c:finite-set), the alphabet, and give the set $A^{\mathbb{Z}}$ of [bi-infinite sequences](c:bi-infinite-sequence) the [product topology](c:product-topology). The [shift map](c:shift-map) $\sigma$ is given by $\sigma(x)_n=x_{n+1}$. A shift space is a closed subset $X\subseteq A^{\mathbb{Z}}$ with $\sigma(X)=X$; equivalently, $X$ is the set of all sequences that avoid a fixed set of forbidden finite words.
examples: The full shift $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ is a shift space.
The golden mean shift, the set of 0-1 sequences with no two consecutive $1$s, is a shift space with the single forbidden word $11$.
The two sequences $\cdots0101\cdots$ and $\cdots1010\cdots$ form a shift space with two points.
Non-example: the set of 0-1 sequences with exactly one $1$ is not closed, because the all-zero sequence is a limit of it and is missing, so it is not a shift space.
